author: Varun Chowdhary
headline: Data Engineer
text:
Data Engineer Interview Questions (2 to 5 Years of Experience)
🚀 Most Repeated Data Engineer Interview Questions (From 20+ Interviews Across Companies)

🥇 1. Spark (MOST ASKED)
 ✔ Spark Architecture
 ✔ DAG vs Lineage
 ✔ Lazy Evaluation
 ✔ Narrow vs Wide transformations
 ✔ Repartition vs Coalesce
 ✔ Broadcast Join
 ✔ Data Skew & Salting
 ✔ Cache vs Persist
 ✔ RDD vs DataFrame
If you master Spark optimization, you clear 40% of interviews.

🥈 2. SQL (Window Functions = Game Changer)
These were extremely common:
 ✔ Second highest salary
 ✔ Top N per department
 ✔ Rank vs Dense_rank vs Row_number
 ✔ LAG / LEAD
 ✔ Running sum / Rolling average
 ✔ 3 consecutive days problem
 ✔ Join output prediction (Inner/Left/Right/Full)
 ✔ Delete duplicates (with & without window functions)
If you’re weak in window functions → fix it immediately.

🥉 3. AWS (Real-World Pipeline Questions)
 ✔ On-prem to AWS migration
 ✔ Incremental load & CDC
 ✔ AWS Glue (Job bookmarking, DPU, DynamicFrame vs DataFrame)
 ✔ S3 versioning & lifecycle policies
 ✔ Redshift distribution styles & COPY command
 ✔ Kinesis vs Firehose
 ✔ Lambda cold start vs hot start

🏗 4. Airflow
 ✔ What is DAG?
 ✔ Executors (Celery/Kubernetes)
 ✔ Scaling 200+ DAGs
 ✔ Task failure handling
 ✔ Scheduler bottlenecks

🧠 5. Data Engineering Concepts
 ✔ OLTP vs OLAP
 ✔ Fact vs Dimension
 ✔ Normalization vs Denormalization
 ✔ ACID properties
 ✔ CAP theorem
 ✔ Partition pruning

author: Anaida Babychen
headline: Data Engineer @ EY GDS| 5 YOE |5x Microsoft Certified |Microsoft Azure | SQL | Microsoft PowerBI | Snowflake| Microsoft Fabric | Python
text:
I wasn't a fan of PySpark until I solved these 10 coding interview questions!

1. DataFrame Operations: Given a DataFrame with missing values, how would you fill null values with the mean of each column?

2. Joins: Write a PySpark query to perform an inner join between two DataFrames on multiple columns.

3. Aggregations: How would you calculate the moving average of a column using PySpark?

4. Window Functions: Given a DataFrame of sales transactions, how do you rank sales per customer within each region using a window function?

5. Filtering & Transformation: Given a DataFrame, how do you filter out rows where a column value appears only once?

6. GroupBy & Aggregations: How would you find the top N most frequently occurring words in a column of a DataFrame?

7. Performance Optimization: How do you repartition a DataFrame efficiently before performing a heavy aggregation?

8. Exploding & Flattening Data: Given a DataFrame with an array column, how do you explode it into multiple rows?

9. Handling Duplicates: How would you remove duplicate rows based on multiple columns while keeping the latest record based on a timestamp column?

10. RDD Transformations: Convert an RDD of tuples into a key-value paired RDD and apply a reduceByKey operation to sum the values for each key.

author: Gowtham. A
headline: PL-300 Certified | BI Lead | Power BI Architect & DBT Data modelling | Expertise in SQL, Power BI, Spotfire, SSRS, Snowflake, ETL, DAX, M Query, Power Automate, DevOps, JIRA, ServiceNow, HL7, and QNXT| 15+ Experience
text:
One of my favorite functions in SQL is LEAD() and LAG() — simple, powerful, and incredibly useful for data analysis.

These window functions help you compare values between rows without using complex self-joins.

🔹 LAG() → looks at the previous row
🔹 LEAD() → looks at the next row

I often use them for:
✅ Comparing current vs previous sales
✅ Finding growth or decline trends
✅ Calculating differences between records
✅ Time-series and sequential analysis

Example use cases:
📊 Month-over-month revenue comparison
📉 Detecting sudden drops or spikes
📈 Tracking performance changes over time

What I love most is how clean and readable the query becomes - no messy joins, just clear logic.
If you work with analytical queries, these functions are absolute game changers.

author: Surbhi Goyal
headline: 100k+ LinkedIn Family | NIT Graduate | 1000+ Resume | Mentor | Spark | Scala | PySpark | Hadoop | Hive | HBase | Azure | AWS | Matillion
text:
I promise you will get 10x better at SQL and Python with these hacks 👇
Thank me later.

𝟏/ 𝐌𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐄𝐋𝐄𝐂𝐓 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐏𝐮𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞
Don’t just write 𝐒𝐄𝐋𝐄𝐂𝐓 *; practice retrieving only relevant columns and rows. It trains your mind to think like a data analyst solving business queries.

𝟐/ 𝐑𝐞𝐰𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬
Take case studies (e.g., “Top-selling products per region”) and write multiple SQL solutions (with and without CTEs, window functions).

𝟑/ 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐘𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐎𝐰𝐧 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞
Use dummy data (from Kaggle or generate with Python) to build a mock e-commerce or banking database in PostgreSQL or MySQL and write queries daily.

𝟒/ 𝐏𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐓𝐢𝐦𝐞-𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐐𝐋
Product companies love asking time-based questions (like weekly retention or daily active users). Get comfortable with 𝐃𝐀𝐓𝐄_𝐓𝐑𝐔𝐍𝐂, 𝐆𝐑𝐎𝐔𝐏 𝐁𝐘 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞, and lagging trends.

𝟓/ 𝐎𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐳𝐞 𝐋𝐢𝐤𝐞 𝐚𝐧 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝗶𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫
Don't just solve queries—optimize them. Use 𝐄𝐗𝐏𝐋𝐀𝐈𝐍 𝐀𝐍𝐀𝐋𝐘𝐙𝐄 to see how your query performs and learn about indexing and subquery performance.

𝟔/ 𝐃𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐒𝐐𝐋 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐞 𝐇𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐭
Spend 30–45 mins daily on platforms like StrataScratch, InterviewQuery, or Mode Analytics SQL tutorials, focusing on real-world problems.
⁣
𝟕/ 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐢𝐧 𝐉𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬, 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐓𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬⁣
When faced with a question, don’t ask "What table?"—ask "How do these tables relate?" Mastering joins is key to solving multi-table business queries.

𝟖/ 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐘𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐌𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬
Maintain a "SQL Misses Log"—every time a query fails or a platform rejects your solution, log what went wrong and rewrite a cleaner version.


𝟗/ 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐬, 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐉𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐒𝐲𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐱: Build micro-projects like:
-Customer churn predictor
-Price optimization mode
-Data pipeline using Pandas + SQLite

𝟏𝟎/ 𝐌𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐬 𝐁𝐞𝐲𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐜𝐬⁣
 
Go deep into:
-.𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐩𝐛𝐲().𝐚𝐠𝐠()⁣
-.𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐞() 𝐯𝐬 𝐣𝐨𝐢𝐧⁣
-𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲 + lambda use cases
-Performance tuning with .loc[] and .query()
